title: Building a Sine Wave That Is the Shadow of a Circle
concept_layer: sine and cosine as projections of uniform circular motion; time↔space equivalence; frequency and amplitude as circle parameters

capture_leaks.two_dimensional_circle: The unit circle is drawn as a 2D loop. In higher dimensions, rotations live on SO(n) — manifolds with more degrees of freedom. Trans_Rotation foreshadowed this with gimbal lock.
capture_leaks.continuous_time: The _process loop ticks in frame-sized discrete steps. The sine wave renders smooth but samples at ~60Hz. Aliasing is inevitable; wave_interference_3d reveals it.
capture_leaks.single_frequency: One sine. But most interesting signals are sums of sines — Fourier. The full story arrives at Synthesis_Lab.
capture_leaks.no_medium: A sine wave needs nothing to propagate in this demo. Add a spring-mass lattice and it becomes waves-through-matter (coupled_oscillator_lattice, then softbodies).
capture_leaks.deterministic_signal: The sine repeats exactly. Add noise and you get real signals (randomness → noise sequences). Add chaos and you get everything else (foundationscrisis).

limit: A sine wave that draws itself is beautiful. It is also a strong claim: that one parameter (frequency) and one function (sin) captures a universe of periodic behavior. Almost every oscillating system — light, sound, pendulums, orbits, heartbeats, quantum states — decomposes into sines via Fourier. The limit is that decomposition assumes linearity. Nonlinear oscillators (later in the curriculum) refuse to be sines.

grammar_alignment.note: OscillationCurve teaches the atomic operation: sin(omega*t). All other wavefunctions operations compose from this one.

biome_alignment.note: The biome now breathes — flowers and trees sway. The catalyst is 'waveform' meaning the player can transform forms into oscillating versions of themselves. Hand verb 'oscillate' lets the player drive the sine parameter directly.

stages.title: From array to wave
stages.thinking: Tutorial_Single taught that an array is space made countable — positions indexed by integer. Now a question: what if the index is continuous instead of discrete? What if, instead of [0], [1], [2], [3], we had a smooth variable t? An array has positions at integer indices; a wave has positions at every real value. The jump from countable to continuous is one of the deepest moves in math. Sin makes that jump visible.
stages.code:
# Tutorial_Single:
#   for i in range(4):
#     cube[i].position = Vector3(0, 0, i * spacing)
#   # 4 discrete samples
#
# Now:
#   for every real t:
#     y(t) = sin(t)
#   # infinite continuous samples
#
# How do you represent a continuous function in code?
# You sample it. Densely. With trails.
# This is what the oscillation curve does.

stages.title: The simplest oscillator
stages.thinking: y = sin(t). One variable in, one variable out. As t flows, y traces a wave that repeats every 2π. This is the primordial oscillator. Everything else — springs, pendulums, light, sound — eventually reduces to this shape via linearization or Fourier decomposition. Start here. Believe it is enough.

stages.title: Render the trail with ImmediateMesh
stages.thinking: To show the wave, we redraw its full history every frame. ImmediateMesh with PRIMITIVE_LINE_STRIP connects consecutive points into a continuous curve. The mesh is rebuilt each _process tick — efficient for a few hundred points, wasteful for millions. But for teaching, clarity beats performance.

stages.title: Show the driver ball at (cos, sin)
stages.thinking: Here is where the unit circle becomes the keystone. A ball rotates in a circle at constant angular velocity. Its Y coordinate as a function of time IS the sine wave. The circle is not a separate demo; the circle IS the wave, seen from above. Project the ball's motion onto the Y axis and you get exactly the sine curve we're drawing to its right.
stages.code:
# driver_ball orbits the unit circle at (cos(t), sin(t))
# Its Y coordinate is exactly what gets plotted on the trail.

func _update_driver_ball() -> void:
	var angle = frequency * time
	driver_ball.position = Vector3(
		cos(angle) * amplitude,       # x on circle
		sin(angle) * amplitude,       # y on circle = y on wave trail
		0
	)

# Watch the ball + trail together.
# The ball's Y is the wave's Y.
# The circle IS the wave, rolled up.

stages.title: Trim the trail so it doesn't grow forever
stages.thinking: points.append + points.pop_front when size exceeds max_points. A sliding window. This is a lesson embedded in the implementation: infinite time can't be represented by an infinite array. You always choose a horizon. max_points=200 at ~60fps means ~3 seconds of visible history. Longer max_points = more memory + more render cost. Shorter = the past vanishes faster. The trade-off is the artifact's critical parameter after frequency.
stages.code:
points.append(new_point)
if points.size() > max_points:
	points.pop_front()

# The array is finite; time is not.
# We see the recent past, no more.
#
# max_points is a choice:
#   200 at 60fps ≈ 3.3 seconds of wave
#   1000 ≈ 16 seconds (more RAM, smoother)
#   50 ≈ 0.8 seconds (feels present-tense, ephemeral)
#
# Every streaming system makes this choice.
# Audio buffers, video scrubbers, chat histories.

stages.title: Expose frequency and amplitude for live tuning
stages.thinking: Two @export parameters. In the editor or via apply_grid_config, the map author or player can change these at runtime. Frequency changes how many cycles fit per unit x-distance. Amplitude changes how tall the wave is. Both are visible immediately because the trail redraws every frame. This is where pedagogy meets play: change a number, see the wave respond. Build intuition through manipulation.

stages.title: The wave forgets where it came from
stages.thinking: A subtle point. The trail renders where the ball has been, but the ball itself doesn't remember. Given the current time t, sin(t) is enough to draw the current y. No accumulated state. No history in the formula. The WAVE is stateful (the trail); the OSCILLATOR is not. This distinction — stateless function vs stateful rendering — matters when you later try to synchronize multiple waves, or rewind time, or predict the future.
stages.code:
# The wave's equation is memoryless:
#   y(t) = A · sin(ω · t)
# Given t, you get y. No history needed.
#
# But the rendered trail IS history:
#   points = [(x₀,y₀), (x₁,y₁), ..., (xₙ,yₙ)]
#
# This is why sin is so useful:
# you can jump to any time, compute instantly,
# without simulating all prior ticks.
#
# Compare to Forces_Foundations:
#   F → a → v → p
#   Each frame depends on the last.
#   You cannot skip to t=100 without simulating.
#
# Sine is jumpable. Integration is not.

stages.title: Give it identity
stages.thinking: An oscillation curve knows what it is. Not a wiggling green line — the shadow of a circle, projected onto time. It also knows its limits: one frequency, one amplitude, one dimension, no medium. Everything that comes next in the wavefunctions sequence (and beyond, into softbodies and into QFEP) is a generalization of this atom. The sine is the prime.
stages.code:

# essence: y(t) = A * sin(omega * t), plotted as trail in 3D
# desire: Watch a sine wave draw itself in space as time flows along the Z axis
# critical_parameter: frequency — controls how many oscillations per unit length

# emerges: the connection between circular motion parameters and wave shape
